title: From TCP bytes to complete messages
summary: Specify and test a framed protocol before building a chat service.
objectives: Distinguish TCP transport from message boundaries
Validate length before allocating
Explain UTF-8 byte lengths and read cancellation
body:
Purpose: messages are an application decision

A chat user types “hello” once, but a TCP receiver is not promised one matching read. TCP supplies an ordered byte stream while a connection works. A read might receive one byte, two messages together, or an incomplete message followed by a disconnect. Framing is our rule for finding message boundaries inside that stream. Our application cannot delegate this rule to packet boundaries or the timing of writes.

Plain-English model

Imagine a parcel carrying a label with its payload size. Our frame has a four-byte, unsigned, big-endian length, followed by that many UTF-8 bytes. Big-endian means the most significant byte comes first: the prefix 00 00 00 02 describes two payload bytes. This analogy explains parsing only; TCP does not preserve parcels and does not promise delivery after a crash. A message is accepted only after every payload byte has arrived and validation succeeds. This protocol allows 1 through 1,024 bytes and rejects control characters. It is a deliberately small text protocol, not an Internet standard.

UTF-8 encodes Unicode characters using variable numbers of bytes. “é” has two UTF-8 bytes here. A Rust String::len() counts bytes, not what a reader perceives as characters. Checking the byte budget before allocating prevents a peer from requesting a four-gigabyte vector. Checking text after the bounded read prevents malformed UTF-8 from leaking into the domain model.

Predict before running

The example below feeds the bytes 00 00 00 02 C3 A9. Will it print one character, two characters, or an error? If the prefix is changed to three, does the missing byte become zero automatically? Explain your prediction before opening the answer.

Prediction explained

It prints é: 2 bytes. Declaring three bytes produces an unexpected end-of-file error because the reader must supply all three. The initialized vector does contain zeros initially, but read_exact does not report success for a partially filled payload.

Small runnable example

Working directory: rust-course/projects. Tokio supplies the asynchronous I/O traits; its version and features are pinned by the workspace.

mise exec -- cargo run -p p09-chat --example frame

Follow the unfamiliar operations

The slice reference is a reader over memory, so the example isolates decoding from actual networking. read_u32 decodes the prefix. The integer is bounded before becoming a vector length. read_exact loops internally until the requested buffer is full or an error occurs. String::from_utf8 validates encoding and takes ownership of the bytes. map_err changes an error into the protocol's I/O error category without pretending it was successful. The ? operator returns early on a failed step.

Intentional failure and first checkpoint

In your learner copy, implement a decoder that calls a single read for the whole payload and incorrectly treats the returned count as a complete message. This is a deliberate runtime logic defect, not a compiler failure. Reproduce it using the fragmented-frame test, then replace that operation with read_exact. Keep the maximum-length check before allocation. The reconstructed 01-framing library contains complete synchronous frame functions and fragmented-reader tests. Compare its byte contract with the final Tokio codec, then reconstruct final to study the complete server after these framing tests pass.

Independent practice

Add tests for a zero-length prefix, a 1,024-byte ASCII payload, an invalid UTF-8 sequence, and a control character. Decide whether line breaks should be legal inside a future chat message. Document the rule before changing both writer and reader validation. Explain why a character-count limit alone does not enforce a wire-byte limit.

Hint 1: identify the boundary

Separate prefix validation from content validation; invalid length should fail before reading a body.

Hint 2: build a fixture

A byte slice implements the reader interface. Prefixes and malformed payloads need no network connection.

Worked approach

Use [0,0,0,0] for empty input and a length of one followed by FF for invalid UTF-8. For the boundary success case, construct 1,024 ASCII bytes and a big-endian prefix. Change the writer to share the same validation helper if you need symmetrical validation; otherwise document that the receiver remains authoritative.

Review and evidence

A deliberate review defect is repeatedly appending reads until “nothing else arrives.” Timing is not framing. The idiomatic design expresses exact lengths and typed errors. Space is O(maximum frame size), and decoding time is O(payload bytes). Tests establish behavior for selected fragments and invalid inputs; they do not prove resistance to every network attack. Run mise exec -- cargo test -p p09-chat and inspect the named boundary tests.

Playbook investigation

Observation: short local messages pass, but messages sometimes lose their first character under load. A plausible guess is a UTF-8 bug. Distinguishing experiment: send ASCII only while splitting the four prefix bytes across separate writes. The same failure disproves the UTF-8 hypothesis. Instrument bytes consumed, not just final text. Another possible cause is cancelling a partially consumed frame read in a select loop and starting over. The server keeps one reader future alive across outgoing writes. That fix preserves decoder progress; it does not create reliable delivery after disconnection.

Mastery check

Without the reference, draw the decoder states, show a partial-prefix trace, explain the memory budget, and implement a bounded frame decoder for a new binary payload. A correct output on one local run is insufficient evidence: explain the failure cases you tested.

When you get stuck

Run mise exec -- cargo test -p p09-chat fragmented_frame_and_utf8 -- --nocapture. Read Tokio AsyncReadExt documentation for the exact operation you used. Request review with the byte fixture, expected state transitions, actual error, and the smallest decoder that reproduces it; do not send only “networking is broken.”

To compare an earlier milestone with the final reference, reconstruct each ID into a different directory. Run the final project’s own boundary fixtures as described in its contract; the chat and workbench use loopback services, and the workbench uses a dedicated disposable journal. These projects do not require PostgreSQL. Passing ordinary unit tests does not establish every network or restart behavior.

Complete earlier milestone source

Read the first-byte EOF branch, the length check before allocation, and the fragmented reader. This is the synchronous byte-contract checkpoint; the Tokio codec adds waiting and cancellation responsibilities later.

title: Bounded chat, slow clients, and shutdown
summary: Own connection tasks and make overload behavior explicit.
objectives: Trace message ownership through reader, channel and writer
Enforce connection/message/time budgets
Explain cancellation versus graceful application delivery
body:
Purpose and service specification

Before reading the reference server, implement this specification: accept at most 32 simultaneous clients on loopback, retain at most 32 chat messages in a shared broadcast queue, reject frames over 1,024 bytes, and disconnect clients whose writes exceed two seconds or whose reads exceed 30 seconds. Disconnect a receiver that has missed messages. Ctrl-C must stop accepting connections and terminate owned tasks. There is no durable history, identity, confidentiality, or delivery acknowledgment. Those are explicit protocol limits, not unfinished error handling.

Plain-English model: admission and backpressure

A resource budget limits work a service is willing to hold. A semaphore is a collection of permits; a live connection owns one until its task ends. A bounded broadcast channel retains a limited sequence of messages for subscribers. Its capacity does not bound everything: each task also owns a read buffer, a write buffer or in-progress frame, runtime state, and operating-system socket buffers. Budget each layer separately before multiplying by connection count.

Backpressure means a downstream limit affects upstream acceptance or speed. This chat chooses disconnects rather than indefinitely slowing every sender for one reader. That is reasonable for disposable chat, but would be wrong for a financial ledger stream that promised every event. A lag notification means a subscriber missed history. Continuing without surfacing that fact would present an incomplete conversation as complete.

Prediction

A broadcast channel holds two messages. A reader has received none when the producer sends three. Does the third send wait forever, does the reader get all three later, or does the reader learn it missed data?

Answer and tempting alternatives

The reader gets a lag error before resuming from retained data. A broadcast channel is not an acknowledgment queue. The third send does not wait for every reader. Our application ends that client's task on lag, so later frames are not silently displayed after a gap.

Run the checkpoint

In rust-course/projects, run the server in one terminal and a client in each of two others. The Python helper uses only the standard library and speaks the actual wire protocol. A browser cannot connect to arbitrary TCP sockets directly.

mise exec -- cargo run -p p09-chat
python3 reference/p09-chat/client.py

Type a short message. Both connected clients should receive it, including the sender. Ctrl-C in the server should end the service. The byte-slice decoder example from the prerequisite remains your small deterministic example. Run mise exec -- cargo test -p p09-chat lag_is_visible to observe the queue policy without relying on socket-buffer timing.

Guided implementation and ownership

Start from your tested frame functions. Add serve with a listener and a watch receiver. The listener owns admission; a JoinSet owns all client tasks. After accept, try_acquire_owned either transfers a permit into a task or rejects that connection immediately. Using an owned permit makes release follow task lifetime, including errors and cancellation. Clone the broadcast sender and subscribe before spawning. Split the stream into read and write halves because independent asynchronous operations need independent ownership.

The reader future is pinned once. Pinning here ensures the future remains at a stable address while being polled; it does not make the stream reliable. The writer selects between that same reader future and incoming broadcast messages. A frame read can consume bytes before returning Pending, so recreating it every time a write wins would lose framing progress. Timeout cancels a read only when the entire connection is being abandoned, which makes that partial state safe to discard.

Deliberate mistake

Replace the bounded channel with an ever-growing Vec per client. A slow reader now makes memory increase with producer speed and elapsed time. This compiles and may look faster in a short test. The failure is operational: overload changes from an explicit disconnect into eventual process memory exhaustion. Restore a finite queue and document what happens when it fills.

Independent practice with staged hints

Measure a client's idle lifetime and implement a different policy: a 10-second deadline for completing the first frame, followed by 60 seconds for later frames. Decide whether outbound traffic should reset the read deadline. Do not just shorten all constants and call the result tested.

Hint 1

Track protocol state explicitly; “connected” and “sent first frame” are different states.

Hint 2

Put a timeout around a whole frame, not each individual byte, or a peer can keep a connection indefinitely by sending one byte per deadline.

Reference reasoning

The timeout belongs to an application phase. Keep a boolean or enum in the dedicated reader and choose the next complete-frame deadline from that phase. Outgoing traffic does not prove the peer is sending valid input, so it should not refresh an inbound deadline unless the specification deliberately says so.

Review, tests, and mastery

A rejected design is to detach tasks and trust them to end. The clearer design retains ownership until shutdown. The current server aborts its connection tasks and drains the JoinSet; it does not wait for application acknowledgments. The loopback test establishes one complete message lifecycle and server termination. Queue tests establish lag semantics, not an OS-specific threshold for a slow socket. Add a targeted short-deadline integration harness if you change those policies. Explain where a message can be lost, why sync locks are unnecessary here, and why finite message size is necessary even with a finite queue.

Playbook investigation

Observation: memory is stable but one client stops receiving under bursts. Guess: “the runtime lost a task.” Capture channel lag counts and connection close reasons, then reduce the producer rate. If lag disappears while the same task structure remains, the lost-task hypothesis lacks support. Reproduce using the deterministic two-slot test before investigating TCP packet captures. The intended fix may be a clearer reconnect notice rather than a larger queue. Larger queues trade delay and memory for tolerance; they cannot rescue a permanently slower consumer.

When you get stuck

Start with mise exec -- cargo test -p p09-chat loopback_and_shutdown -- --nocapture. If it hangs, add temporary tracing at accept, frame completion, broadcast receive, and shutdown. Share the lifecycle trace and your predicted owner of each task. Use the Tokio broadcast documentation to check whether lag closes a receiver automatically; application code decides that.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Scope and invariants: a loopback text broadcast service,32 clients,32 retained messages,1,024-byte validated frames, finite read/write deadlines. No authentication, TLS, durable delivery, or historical replay is promised. Why this design: explicit framing and owned connection tasks make partial reads, resource release, and shutdown traceable. An owned permit couples admission to connection lifetime. Concrete habits: validate before allocation; retain partially consumed decoder state; bound task and message counts; identify deliberate failures separately from the recommended implementation.

Alternative: per-client bounded mpsc queues allow individual policies and accounting but require more queue ownership and fan-out code. For a durable stream, use sequence IDs and a persistent replay protocol instead of enlarging a disposable chat queue. Evidence: fragmented bytes, oversize, truncation, lag, and loopback shutdown tests establish selected protocol cases. They do not prove every transport failure or denial-of-service scenario. Evolution threshold: add a maintained authentication/TLS boundary before any nonlocal use; add explicit delivery semantics before users depend on history.

mise exec -- cargo test --locked --manifest-path learner-work/checkpoints/p09-chat/final/Cargo.toml

To compare an earlier milestone with the final reference, reconstruct each ID into a different directory. Run the final project’s own boundary fixtures as described in its contract; the chat and workbench use loopback services, and the workbench uses a dedicated disposable journal. These projects do not require PostgreSQL. Passing ordinary unit tests does not establish every network or restart behavior.

Observe shutdown state before waiting

A watch channel retains the latest state; it is not just a sequence of notifications. The initial value is considered seen by a new receiver, so waiting for changed() alone misses a stop already set to true. The server now inspects borrow_and_update() before each wait. A true value stops admission, false only means keep running, and losing every sender also requests shutdown. The borrowed guard ends before any await.

Predict what happens for an initially true channel, then run the two shutdown regressions. One requires the server to finish without a second change; the other exchanges real frames after false notifications and checks that sender closure drains the server. Their two-second deadlines detect a stalled test; they do not claim an operational latency bound. The main function owns a pinned server future and selects it against Ctrl-C in the same task. On Ctrl-C it signals shutdown and awaits that same server future, avoiding a detached signal-watcher task. If signal registration fails, it still drains the server before returning the error.

Read the pinned Tokio watch documentation and select! cancellation rules. Explain why retaining the future matters, and why a false state notification must not mean stop. Working directory: projects. Run mise exec -- cargo test -p p09-chat --locked.

Startup output is an ordinary I/O boundary

A startup message can fail when a pipe closes or an output device rejects a write. The entry point now uses a locked stdout writer, writeln! and flush, propagating I/O errors with ? before it begins the server future. Printing macros such as println! panic on output errors; they are not the error-handling policy for this service. A write failure therefore exits unsuccessfully without a detached connection or signal task. The locked writer's scope ends before any await.

Predict the closed-pipe result before reading the real process evidence: it is an ordinary BrokenPipe error, not a panic. The separate lifecycle experiment exchanges a valid framed message, sends SIGINT only to the owned server process, and observes exit zero. These are tested paths, not a proof of every operating-system shutdown schedule.

title: HTTP contracts and authorization boundaries
summary: Turn requests into validated domain operations and safe responses.
objectives: Separate authentication from authorization
Read HTTP requests and status codes
Use Axum extractors and explicit error responses
body:
Purpose: an interface another program can trust

The issue tracker lets a client create, list, and close team issues. An HTTP API is a contract between programs, not merely a set of function names. The contract includes method, path, headers, body schema, status, error shape, and permission rules. A client must be able to distinguish invalid input, missing identity, forbidden action, stale revision, and temporarily unavailable storage without inspecting a Rust stack trace.

Plain-English model

HTTP adds request and response semantics over a transport. A request contains a method such as GET or POST, a target path, headers, and sometimes a body. JSON is a text serialization format that represents values; it does not by itself validate business meaning. A JSON number may be syntactically valid while being an impossible page size. TLS encrypts and authenticates the transport endpoint when configured correctly. Our localhost lab uses plain HTTP and public teaching identities, so it is not a deployed identity system.

Authentication establishes who a caller is. Authorization decides what that caller may do to this resource. The demo fixtures map three explicit bearer strings to two teams and reader/writer roles. They exist to test authorization branches deterministically. They are not passwords, not cryptographic tokens, and not a recommended login design. For a deployment, use a maintained identity integration with an established protocol such as OpenID Connect, validate its issuer and audience, and preserve the same resource checks. Do not replace this lab with a homemade signature or password scheme.

Predict the boundary

A team-one writer knows a team-two issue ID. Should possession of that ID allow closing it? Should hiding the close button in the UI be sufficient? Predict what the API should return.

Answer

The server must constrain the operation to the authenticated actor's team. This API returns not-found for an inaccessible issue, avoiding confirmation of another team's resource. UI controls improve usability but are not a security boundary. Reader permissions also need server enforcement even when the client sends a valid writer-shaped JSON body.

Small example: validation before transport

Run the validation example without a database. The first title becomes “fix login”; the whitespace-only title produces a domain validation error.

mise exec -- cargo run -p p10-issues --example validation

Read the handler shape

Axum's State extractor supplies shared application resources, HeaderMap supplies request headers, Path parses route values, and Json deserializes the body. Body-consuming extractors belong last in the handler arguments. The handler validates identity and title, awaits a parameterized database operation, then returns a typed status plus JSON. IntoResponse centralizes application error rendering. The public response says storage is unavailable; internal query details stay in the local service log.

The 4,096-byte body limit bounds deserialization input. The title rule independently limits meaningful title characters. Those are different constraints. Axum's built-in JSON rejection responses are framework responses; this reference does not claim one uniform custom error schema for every malformed transport request. A production API may wrap extractor rejections into its chosen problem format.

Guided checkpoint

In a learner copy, first implement validate_title and its two tests. Then implement actor mapping and a test that a reader cannot write. The reconstructed HTTP milestone provides the complete /issues/validate router and handler without storing issues. Use it to test extraction and role checks. Reconstruct the final checkpoint for complete database-backed create/list/close handlers after the SQL lesson; do not create empty handler stubs and call them a working checkpoint. This order gives you a runnable domain checkpoint before a database is available. Do not replace expected input errors with unwrap.

Deliberate mistake and practice

Intentionally remove the team predicate from the close lookup in your working copy. It still compiles. The cross-team integration test must now fail. Restore it before continuing. Next design a “reopen” operation: specify permissions, legal state transition, expected revision behavior, and whether retrying the same request is success or conflict. Decide those semantics before implementing the route.

Hint 1

Start with a table of actor role, owning team, current state, and expected revision.

Hint 2

A state transition is different from assigning a boolean. Decide whether reopening an already open issue is meaningful.

Reference approach

Keep a resource-scoped lookup and optimistic revision check inside the transaction. Give reopen its own operation with writer permission. Reject stale revisions consistently, update the audit row with the new revision, and test cross-team access independently from state conflicts. An idempotent command ID is an alternative contract, but requires persisted command results.

Review and evidence

A deliberate authorization defect is accepting team_id in the JSON body as authority. A clearer boundary derives team membership from server-side identity and ignores client claims of authority. Validation tests prove selected inputs are handled. The PostgreSQL route test proves actual reader and cross-team denials through the router. Neither proves a secure login flow because no such flow exists in the reference. Explain why TLS, authentication, authorization, CSRF protection for cookie-based clients, and input validation solve different problems.

Playbook investigation

Observation: a valid writer sees 404 for one issue while another writer can close it. A tempting guess is “the migration lost the row.” Query only the dedicated test database to confirm the row exists, then inspect its team and the fixture identity. Reproduce with both identities through HTTP. A row existing globally does not imply it belongs in this caller's visible set. The correct fix may be using the intended identity, not deleting authorization. Record that disproven hypothesis and retain a regression test for the boundary.

Mastery check

Explain an entire request from bytes to extractor to domain validation to transaction to response. Add a permission rule without relying on UI code, and show one denied test that would catch accidentally removing it.

When you get stuck

Run mise exec -- cargo test -p p10-issues title_and_roles. Inspect method, path, content-type, and exact public fixture identity before changing handlers. Consult the pinned Axum extractor documentation. A useful review request includes a permission matrix, a minimal HTTP request, the expected status, and the test that fails.

title: Tables, indexes, transactions, and migrations
summary: Make state changes correct when requests overlap and storage fails.
objectives: Model keys, constraints and indexes
Explain transaction atomicity and isolation
Separate compile-time query metadata from deployed schema
body:
Purpose and acceptance criteria

Closing an issue must update its state and write an audit record together. If the audit insert fails, the issue must remain open. Two simultaneous requests with the same expected revision must not both claim to close it. Before looking at the implementation, write those two criteria as timelines. This is the point where “save some data” becomes a concurrency contract.

Plain-English model: related facts

A relational database stores rows in tables. A column has a type and may have constraints. A primary key uniquely identifies a row; a foreign key ties one table's value to a referenced row. Our issue audit points to the issue it describes. A CHECK constraint rejects invalid persisted values even when a future client forgets application validation. SQL is the language for selecting and changing these rows. Its evaluation model is about sets of rows, not the iteration order of a Rust vector.

An index is an auxiliary search structure. The (team_id,id) index supports locating one team's issues after a cursor. It costs storage and update work; adding every imaginable index can slow writes. A transaction groups statements into an atomic committed unit. Atomicity does not mean every intermediate read is globally isolated from all concurrent activity. PostgreSQL's default Read Committed isolation gives statement snapshots. Explicit row locking in our transition makes competing closers wait and recheck the relevant state.

Prediction with a transaction timeline

A starts a transaction, changes the issue, and attempts an audit insert that violates a uniqueness constraint. A then returns an error and drops its transaction. B reads the issue afterward. Does B see the changed state? Now consider A committing successfully but losing its HTTP response. Is the client entitled to assume the close failed?

Answer

The failed transaction does not commit the change, so B sees the previously committed state. A lost HTTP response is different: the database may have committed. The client must reconcile state or use a persisted idempotency key. Network uncertainty cannot be converted into proof of rollback.

Small runnable schema checkpoint

Read the migration, then run the database integration test against an explicitly disposable database named rust_course_test_issues. Never point this test at a real application database; it intentionally clears the two test tables. The fixture parses SQLx connection options and requires the exact database name, a literal loopback IP or an absolute local Unix socket path. Each connected session checks SELECT current_database() before migrations or table resets. These checks catch common wrong-target mistakes; a name alone does not prove the database is disposable.

createdb rust_course_test_issues
export COURSE_TEST_DATABASE_URL="postgresql:///rust_course_test_issues?host=/tmp&user=$USER"
mise exec -- cargo test -p p10-issues --test postgres -- --ignored

If the database already exists, do not recreate or drop it blindly. Inspect its ownership and contents. If ownership is uncertain, use a fresh isolated PostgreSQL cluster; do not repurpose or drop that database. The fixture guard accepts the exact documented name in that separate cluster, not a substring embedded elsewhere in a URL. The quoted URL uses your shell user as the PostgreSQL role; replace $USER if your database role differs. On systems whose socket directory differs, adjust the URL. PostgreSQL is an external local prerequisite; a passing ordinary Cargo test does not imply these ignored database tests ran.

Guided project step

Implement the migration exactly, then walk through close_issue in the reference. Begin a transaction; select the row using both ID and actor team with FOR UPDATE; compare its revision; update the issue; insert the audit row; commit. Every operation uses the same transaction connection. Accidentally calling execute(pool) for the audit would move it outside the transaction and break the guarantee.

Values are passed with .bind() into PostgreSQL placeholders $1, $2, and so on. Do not interpolate titles into SQL text. Parameters represent values, not table names or arbitrary SQL fragments. The title “Alice's bug” is a useful test because the apostrophe is ordinary data and should not change query syntax. The SQLx 0.9 API accepts static SQL strings directly and deliberately makes dynamic SQL construction explicit.

Deliberate mistake

Temporarily remove the transaction and execute the state update before an audit insert that will fail. The rollback assertion should fail because the issue is already closed. Restore the transaction, then verify the same injected audit conflict leaves the issue open. Compilation cannot detect this semantic difference.

Query verification and offline metadata

The default project uses runtime queries so it builds without a running database. This does not provide compile-time SQL verification. The optional verified-query feature contains a real query! example that checks a count query against the schema visible at build time. With the schema migrated, run the following command. SQLx CLI0.9.0 is the matching tool. From projects/reference/p10-issues, run mise exec -- cargo sqlx prepare -- --features verified-query to generate package-local metadata, then mise exec -- cargo sqlx prepare --check -- --features verified-query to compare it with the current preparation schema. The package includes the actual generated .sqlx/query-*.json file for the count query. Run SQLX_OFFLINE=true mise exec -- cargo check --features verified-query from that package to build using the metadata without contacting PostgreSQL. Generated metadata must be reviewed and committed with schema changes; an empty metadata directory proves nothing.

export DATABASE_URL="postgresql:///rust_course_test_issues?host=/tmp&user=$USER"
mise exec -- cargo check -p p10-issues --features verified-query

Offline metadata describes the schema used during preparation. It cannot inspect the live deployment database, prove migrations ran there, or prove transactional business rules. The verification report records actual metadata preparation, prepare --check, and forced offline recompilation for this optional feature. The default runtime queries still rely on database integration tests for schema validation.

Practice, review, and evidence

Add a title-change transaction with revision checking. Decide whether the audit stores the old title, the new title, or both. Then explain the retention and privacy implications. A limited alternative puts all validation in Rust; a robust design also uses constraints for durable invariants and parameter binding for SQL syntax separation.

Hint 1

List facts that must remain true even if two requests overlap.

Hint 2

Keep audit and update on &mut *tx; test the failure between them.

Reference reasoning

Use the same lock-and-revision transition, add the chosen audit fields through a new migration, and test both successful history and forced rollback. Do not edit an applied migration just to hide a mismatch; migration checksums exist to expose changed history.

Playbook investigation and mastery

Observation: an issue is closed with no audit. The first hypothesis is a database durability failure. Inspect transaction IDs and the code's executor arguments before blaming storage. If the audit uses the pool while the update uses a transaction, a controlled constraint failure reproduces the symptom without crashing PostgreSQL. That disproves the crash hypothesis for this reproduction. Fix the transaction boundary, document that a lost commit acknowledgment remains uncertain, and explain the distinction without the reference.

When you get stuck

Run the ignored integration test explicitly and read the exact SQLSTATE in the local log. Use psql "$COURSE_TEST_DATABASE_URL" only for the isolated database. Consult PostgreSQL 18 transaction isolation and SQLx0.9 transaction docs. Ask for review with the two-request timeline, SQL statements, transaction boundaries, and failed assertion.

Reconstruct this runnable checkpoint

Working directory: course root. This creates a complete separate source tree; it refuses an existing destination. Run the checkpoint tests before following the guided edits. The checkpoint contract and engineering decisions state exactly which features exist.

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p10 final
mise exec -- cargo test --locked --manifest-path learner-work/checkpoints/p10-issues/final/Cargo.toml

To compare an earlier milestone with the final reference, reconstruct each ID into a different directory. The final database integration checks still require the explicitly isolated database described in this lesson; ordinary cargo test does not execute ignored database tests.

Investigate the test target before changing it

A URL can contain rust_course_test in a username or application_name while selecting an unrelated database. Predict whether that old substring guard would reject the wrong target; the pure guard tests demonstrate that it would not. The corrected helper reads SQLx's effective database and transport after parsing URL overrides, rejects a mismatched name before connecting, and checks the server-reported database on every connection. The regression matrix uses strings only and does not contact those rejected hosts. A separate fresh Unix-socket-only PostgreSQL cluster verifies the accepted integration path.

Read SQLx 0.9 connection options and PostgreSQL 18's current_database function. These are defensive checks against mistakes, not an ownership proof or permission to reset a database containing learner data. Prefer the owned fixture runner in the verification evidence when repeating destructive acceptance tests.

title: An issue API you can test at its boundaries
summary: Integrate routes, database migrations, pagination, and operational failure handling.
objectives: Implement cursor pagination with a stable order
Test authorization through the actual router
Plan schema evolution and bounded database use
body:
Purpose and independent specification

Complete the issue tracker using the contracts from the previous lessons. A writer creates a trimmed, nonempty title of at most 200 Unicode scalar values. A reader lists only its team's issues. Results are ordered by ascending ID, with a positive limit no greater than 100 and an optional exclusive after cursor. Closing requires a matching revision and produces one audit row. Read these criteria first, then implement against your own tests before opening the reference source.

Plain-English model: boundaries compose

A boundary is where one set of assumptions becomes another: HTTP bytes become a typed request, an identity becomes permissions, a domain transition becomes SQL, and rows become JSON. Testing the pure title validator is useful but does not prove that the route calls it. Testing SQL alone does not prove the handler applies the right actor team. An integration test deliberately crosses several boundaries and checks the behavior visible to a caller.

Pagination limits one response's work. Offset pagination skips a number of rows, which can become costly and unstable when earlier rows change. Our keyset cursor says “give me IDs greater than this known ID.” Together with ORDER BY id, it defines a predictable continuation. It is not a frozen snapshot across pages: newly inserted issues may appear later, and filters can change membership. Say which user experience you support instead of calling every ordered page consistent.

Predict

The last returned ID is 20. Between page requests, someone deletes ID 3 and inserts ID 30. With after=20, should the next page repeat ID20? Does deleting ID3 shift the meaning of the cursor? What would an offset of 20 mean instead?

Reasoning

The cursor excludes20 and compares key values, so deleting3 does not shift it. ID30 may appear if it belongs to this team. An offset counts currently visible rows before the response and can skip or repeat logical positions as data changes. Neither method alone guarantees a snapshot of an earlier moment.

Runnable service checkpoint

Use a separate local application database, not the disposable integration-test database. The server runs embedded migrations on startup, limits its pool to five connections, and binds loopback port4110. This default makes migrations convenient locally; a deployment may use a separate migration step with narrower runtime permissions.

createdb rust_course_issues
export DATABASE_URL="postgresql:///rust_course_issues?host=/tmp&user=$USER"
mise exec -- cargo run -p p10-issues
# Another terminal:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer demo-team1-writer" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Investigate timeout"}' http://127.0.0.1:4110/issues
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer demo-team1-reader" "http://127.0.0.1:4110/issues?limit=20"

Expected behavior: create returns201 with a generated issue ID and revision0; list returns an array visible to team1. A reader's create returns403. Do not paste real credentials into these fixture commands. Start with the pure validation example if PostgreSQL is unavailable.

Explain the integration test

The test uses Tower's oneshot to send a real request through the Axum router without opening a network port. This exercises routing, extraction, permission checks, handlers, and response construction. It still uses an actual isolated PostgreSQL database. The test inserts a title containing an apostrophe, checks another team's empty list, denies cross-team close, checks a successful close, rejects a stale retry, and verifies pagination. Finally it forces an audit uniqueness failure and confirms rollback.

Deliberate mistake and guided increment

Remove ORDER BY id in your learner query and run the test. It may still pass on a tiny table. This is an instructive limitation of example-based tests: observed order is not a promised order. Restore the explicit ordering, then write a three-page test with multiple teams, enough rows to cross boundaries, and IDs tracked in a set. Assert no duplicates and the specified ascending order. The implementation checkpoint is the complete router plus migration; the improvement checkpoint is your expanded pagination evidence.

Independent design decisions

Add a closed/open filter while preserving cursor semantics. Decide whether the cursor should be reusable with a different filter. Write the API rule, a client example, and a test before implementing. Then design a second migration adding an optional assignee. Explain what old binaries do when the new column exists, whether new binaries can read old rows, and when backfill work must happen.

Hint 1

The cursor is part of a query, not just an integer. Consider encoding filter context if accidental reuse matters.

Hint 2

An additive nullable column allows old rows and old writers during a transition. Enforcing a new required value immediately can break them.

Reference approach

For this small API, document that clients must preserve filters across pages and reject invalid filter values. Add a nullable assignee through a new migration and keep authorization based on team membership, not assignee identity. For a larger public API, use an opaque cursor carrying versioned query context and validate it with a maintained mechanism if tamper resistance is required.

Review and evidence

A happy-path curl session is a useful smoke test, but insufficient boundary evidence. A stronger review asks what authorization predicate protects every query, what bounds every collection, what happens when acquiring a connection times out, and how deployment schema is known. The five-connection pool bounds active database connections. A separate16-request semaphore and five-second handler/body deadline bound admitted HTTP work; they do not replace operating-system connection limits or a deployment rate policy. This reference has no deployment TLS/authentication integration. Its local scope and remaining limits must remain visible.

Playbook investigation

Observation: requests stall while CPU stays low. Misleading evidence: the database process is alive and /health returns200. Hypothesize exhausted pool, slow queries, lock waits, or a handler retaining a transaction. Distinguish them with pool acquisition timing and PostgreSQL activity/lock inspection in the test environment. A responsive health route only proves the runtime can answer that route. If an intentionally held row lock reproduces close latency while reads work, “CPU shortage” is disproven. Fix the transaction lifetime and add request deadlines; do not increase pool size without measuring the database budget.

Mastery check

Demonstrate a denied request, a rolled-back transition, and a paginated traversal. Review the API as if its author were absent. Name one guarantee established by each test and one important behavior not covered.

When you get stuck

Run mise exec -- cargo test -p p10-issues --test postgres -- --ignored --nocapture with the isolated database URL. Compare actual status and JSON before reading server logs. Include schema version, actor role, cursor, expected revision, and the minimal failing request in a review request.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Scope and invariants: local two-team issue state, permission checks on every domain operation, bounded page/body/pool sizes, atomic issue-and-audit transitions, revision conflict detection. Why this design: pure validation can run without infrastructure, while SQL constraints and transaction-scoped row locks protect durable facts under concurrent requests. Concrete habits: derive authority server-side; bind SQL values; keep all transaction statements on the same connection; test denied requests and injected rollback through the actual router.

Alternative: an optimistic conditional UPDATE can reduce explicit lock code for a simple transition, but the associated audit and returned conflict semantics still require a transaction. Evidence: actual PostgreSQL integration tests and prepared query metadata are recorded separately from pure unit checks. Neither verifies a production identity provider or live deployment schema. Evolution threshold: add maintained authentication/TLS, deployment connection/rate limits, query-plan measurement, and migration rollout checks before multiuser deployment. Public fixture tokens are not secret credentials or a security claim.

Reconstruct this runnable checkpoint

Working directory: course root. This creates a complete separate source tree; it refuses an existing destination. Run the checkpoint tests before following the guided edits. The checkpoint contract and engineering decisions state exactly which features exist.

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p10 final
mise exec -- cargo test --locked --manifest-path learner-work/checkpoints/p10-issues/final/Cargo.toml

To compare an earlier milestone with the final reference, reconstruct each ID into a different directory. The final database integration checks still require the explicitly isolated database described in this lesson; ordinary cargo test does not execute ignored database tests.

Keep startup and shutdown failures visible

The binary reads DATABASE_URL through a deliberately redacted conversion: both missing and non-Unicode values produce a fixed configuration message. A VarError::NotUnicode contains the original operating-system value, so forwarding its Debug representation could expose a credential. Do not solve an encoding failure by logging the entire value. The child-process regression uses a synthetic marker and invalid byte, and confirms neither the marker nor a panic appears before any database connection.

Required startup output uses fallible Write operations. The main task retains one server future, selects it against Ctrl-C, and signals a watch channel to request graceful shutdown. IntoFuture converts Axum's awaitable server builder into the future that select! polls explicitly; tokio::pin! lets the same in-progress future be awaited afterward. After either normal or error completion, the pool is closed before the saved server or signal error is returned. A signal-registration failure requests shutdown too. No detached signal watcher is needed. See the scoped output evidence for the actual checks and the database-service runtime limits.

title: Partial failure, idempotency, and the outbox
summary: Reason about work that can happen even when its acknowledgment is lost.
objectives: Distinguish operation outcome from observed response
Design idempotency keys and conflict rules
Explain transactional outbox and external-effect limits
body:
Purpose: retry without accidental duplication

A report job reaches a worker, the worker writes its result, and the acknowledgment disappears. The caller sees a timeout. Should it retry? The important fact is not that the timeout occurred; it is that the caller cannot tell whether the work happened. Distributed engineering starts with this gap between reality and observation. Rust's memory safety cannot remove it.

Plain-English model

At-least-once delivery allows repeated delivery while aiming to avoid permanent loss under stated recovery assumptions. At-most-once avoids repeated attempts but may lose work. Neither phrase alone defines how an external action behaves. Idempotency means repeating an operation with the same logical identity produces the same intended effect rather than an additional effect. It is a property of the operation and its storage boundary, not a property supplied automatically by HTTP or a queue.

Our scheduler assigns a bounded textual job ID. Submitting the same ID and same payload is accepted as a retry. Reusing the ID with a different payload is a conflict. A unique database key makes simultaneous duplicate submissions meet at a single storage constraint. A local in-memory “seen IDs” set would forget history after restart. A payload hash can be useful, but the project stores and compares the bounded payload directly so the teaching model does not need to invent a hashing protocol.

Prediction: where is the atomic boundary?

A worker sends an email, then writes “done” to PostgreSQL. It crashes between those actions. On restart, the job is delivered again. Does a unique jobs table row guarantee the recipient sees only one email?

Answer

No. The external mail system and our database did not share a transaction. The recipient may receive two messages. A downstream idempotency contract, a deduplicating effect store, or a business rule tolerating duplicates is required. Merely naming a job “exactly once” changes nothing.

Small runnable evidence

The scheduler's integration test enqueues the same job twice, rejects a conflicting payload, expires a lease, redelivers it, rejects a stale completion, and commits one database effect. It uses an explicit logical timestamp, so the failure schedule is deterministic rather than dependent on sleeping. First read the test and predict each returned boolean.

createdb rust_course_test_scheduler
export COURSE_SCHEDULER_TEST_DATABASE_URL="postgresql:///rust_course_test_scheduler?host=/tmp&user=$USER"
mise exec -- cargo test -p p14-scheduler --test postgres -- --ignored

Guided implementation

Implement enqueue before the worker. The function starts an admission transaction and acquires a transaction-scoped advisory lock. It first looks up the logical ID and compares any stored payload, returning false only for an exact retry. Otherwise it checks the retained-row budget, inserts the unique ID and payload, and commits. The lock serializes the count-and-insert decision across callers; the unique key remains a durable invariant. The caller can then distinguish newly accepted work from an already known command without creating another durable row. Add tests for empty IDs, oversized IDs, and a conflicting payload before introducing concurrent workers.

Next inspect complete. It locks the job, verifies status, lease token, and lease expiry at the authority decision, reads the immutable payload from that locked durable row, inserts into job_effects under a unique job key, and marks the job done in the same transaction. This demonstrates one database-local deduplicated effect. It does not generalize automatically to sending money, publishing to a broker, or invoking an external HTTP endpoint.

The transactional outbox pattern

An outbox is a table of events written in the same transaction as a domain change. A relay later reads unpublished entries and delivers them. If the relay crashes after delivery but before marking an entry delivered, the event can be sent again. Consumers therefore still need idempotency or deduplication. The gain is avoiding the gap where a domain change commits but the intent to publish is lost. The reference scheduler's effect table illustrates transactional coupling; it does not include a production outbox relay. Implementing one is an independent extension with its own acceptance criteria.

Deliberate mistake and independent practice

Replace the database uniqueness rule with a HashSet initialized when the worker starts. Demonstrate that a restart permits a duplicate effect. Then design an outbox entry containing event ID, aggregate ID, payload version, and payload. Specify how long deduplication records must live and what happens when a caller retries after retention expires.

Hint 1

Draw every durable write and every external action on separate vertical process lines.

Hint 2

Mark crash points before and after each arrow. Ask what survives and what the next process can observe.

Reference reasoning

Store outbox intent with the domain transaction, retry relay delivery with the same event ID, and have the consumer transaction insert a deduplication record together with its own domain effect. Retention is part of the contract: forgetting an ID reopens the possibility of an old retry becoming a new effect. Long retention has storage and privacy costs.

Review and evidence

A rejected retry design catches every error and retries immediately. A careful design classifies retryable conditions, caps attempts, delays repeated work, and preserves logical identity. The current scheduler demonstrates bounded attempts and a deterministic delay; randomized jitter for large fleets is an extension. Tests establish selected duplicate and stale-worker behaviors in PostgreSQL. They do not prove behavior under every database failover or uncertain external response.

Playbook investigation

Observation: a report exists twice, yet the queue dashboard shows one completed job. A plausible hypothesis is duplicate enqueue. Inspect job IDs and attempt tokens. If both effects share one job ID but came from two lease attempts, duplicate enqueue is disproven. Reproduce a crash after the external effect and before completion. The fix belongs at the effect boundary, not merely at submission. Record what downstream idempotency guarantees are available and which failure window remains if none exist.

Mastery check

Explain why an acknowledgment is evidence of an observed outcome, not the outcome itself. Draw an outbox timeline with a duplicate-delivery crash window. Implement a deduplicated effect with a conflicting-payload rule and defend the retention policy without copying the reference.

When you get stuck

Run the single scheduler integration test with its dedicated URL, then inspect jobs and job_effects in that database. Label every proposed retry with its logical ID. Ask for review using a failure timeline and the exact transaction boundaries, not only the phrase “exactly once.”

Reconstruct this runnable checkpoint

mise exec -- cargo test --locked --manifest-path learner-work/checkpoints/p14-scheduler/01-lease-model/Cargo.toml

To compare an earlier milestone with the final reference, reconstruct each ID into a different directory. The final database integration checks still require the explicitly isolated database described in this lesson; ordinary cargo test does not execute ignored database tests.

Complete earlier milestone source

Time is supplied as a nondecreasing logical tick. Compare the current token and deadline before allowing completion. Observe how exact enqueue retries remain successful when admission is full.

Authority is not every field in a returned value

Lease is an owned observation returned to a worker. Its public payload and attempts fields are convenient for display, but callers can modify them. Completion must read the payload from the locked database row; retry delay must use the persisted attempt count. A focused test keeps the correct ID and token while substituting a payload and changing attempts from 1 to 3. The reference still writes the original payload and schedules the first-failure delay. Before the correction, the substituted payload became the durable effect. This disproves the tempting claim that checking a token makes every field beside it authoritative.

The same test injects a constraint failure during effect insertion and verifies that no effect appears and the job remains running. Removing the fixture constraint permits completion under the still-current lease. This is evidence for the actual database-local transaction boundary; it does not test an external email or outbox relay. Independent review of the implementation remains pending.

title: Leases, retries, cancellation, and recovery
summary: Build a durable local queue with explicit stale-worker behavior.
objectives: Use lease tokens to reject stale completion
Bound execution and retries
Specify clock and cancellation assumptions
body:
Specification before implementation

Build a queue backed by PostgreSQL. A job has an immutable ID and payload, a state, an attempt count, a lease token, a next-attempt time, and a lease deadline. At most one local worker executes at a time. Claiming a job increments its token and attempt count. A lease lasts five seconds. After three failed or abandoned attempts the job becomes dead. A stale worker must not record completion. Cancellation revokes a pending or running lease, but cannot undo an external action that already occurred.

Plain-English model: temporary authority

A lease is permission that expires. It is useful because a crashed process cannot voluntarily return its work. After the deadline, another worker may claim the same job. This creates an overlap risk: the original worker may be slow rather than dead. A fencing token is a monotonically increasing identifier that lets a resource reject an older owner. Our completion transaction compares the job's current token with the worker's token. An external service would need to enforce a corresponding rule or an idempotency contract; our database check cannot control an unrelated process.

The scheduler uses millisecond timestamps in an explicit time domain. Deterministic tests pass logical times to complete; complete_with_clock instead receives a clock function and calls it after acquiring the job row lock. The binary passes now_ms, so pool and row-lock waits cannot preserve an earlier unexpired timestamp for the authority decision. Claim time is sampled before its database operation, which can shorten the useful lease if admission waits. Neither path models multiple machines with skewed clocks. A real multi-host lease design should use a clearly chosen time authority and define clock-jump behavior. A lease timestamp is not the same thing as a duration measured by a monotonic timer.

Prediction

Worker A claims job J with token1 at time0. A pauses. At time5,000, B claims J with token2. A wakes at5,001 and tries to complete. Which worker may commit the effect? What if A already sent an email before pausing?

Answer

Only token2 matches current authority, so A's database completion returns false. That prevents stale database mutation. It cannot retract an email already sent. The two questions belong to different effect boundaries, which is why lease ownership and idempotency both matter.

Runnable checkpoint

The migration creates jobs and a database-local effect table. The binary starts a loopback API and one owned worker. It is intentionally small enough that you can trace every transition. Use a scheduler-specific database because its migration sequence is independent from the issue tracker.

createdb rust_course_scheduler
export SCHEDULER_DATABASE_URL="postgresql:///rust_course_scheduler?host=/tmp&user=$USER"
mise exec -- cargo run -p p14-scheduler
# Another terminal:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer demo-operator" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"id":"report-1","payload":"synthetic report"}' http://127.0.0.1:4114/jobs

Expected output includes the job ID, lease token, and whether the effect transaction committed. Submitting the identical payload again returns inserted:false. The public fixture credential is an authorization teaching aid, not deployable authentication.

Guided implementation and unfamiliar SQL

Implement enqueue with its serialized admission budget and duplicate semantics first. Then implement claim as a single update whose subquery chooses the earliest eligible row. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets concurrent claimers skip already locked candidates instead of all waiting on the same job. It does not by itself guarantee fairness. The UPDATE records the new authority and returns a typed Lease. A JoinHandle owns the worker task; shutdown signals it and awaits its completion.

Failure schedules the next attempt using a capped exponential delay. The reference has one worker, at most three attempts per job, and an admission cap of10,000 retained job rows. Enqueue takes a transaction-scoped advisory lock before checking capacity and inserting, so concurrent submissions cannot race past the limit. Exact retries still succeed at capacity; new jobs receive429. This simple serialized admission decision favors a checkable local budget over maximum enqueue throughput. Completed rows retain identity history; an archival and retention policy is required before this budget fills. The HTTP body and payload are separately bounded. A bounded execution count alone would not bound lifetime storage.

Deliberate mistake

Remove the token comparison from completion in a learner copy. The stale-worker assertion must fail. Next remove the lease deadline comparison while keeping the token. A worker whose lease has expired at the authority decision but has not yet been reclaimed could now be accepted. Decide whether that is acceptable in your specification; the reference deliberately rejects it. The row remains locked across the accepted database effect and completion; this does not promise that the eventual transaction commit occurs before the wall-clock deadline. These are application races, not Rust data races, so safe Rust still compiles.

Independent practice

Implement a paused state and replace the fixed retained-row budget with a reviewed retention policy. Specify whether paused jobs retain leases and whether cancellation wins against a completion transaction already holding the row lock. Then design a heartbeat renewal operation that cannot revive an expired lease. Use a deterministic timestamp in tests and avoid sleeping to “make the race happen.”

Hint 1

Write a transition table with source state, required token, time condition, destination, and durable writes.

Hint 2

A renewal must compare both token and unexpired deadline atomically. Updating only by job ID lets old workers steal authority back.

Reference reasoning

Renew with a conditional UPDATE requiring running status, the same token, and a deadline greater than now. Decide a maximum total lease age to stop permanent extension. For queue admission, make the limit race-safe with a serialized admission counter or another explicit transactional mechanism; a count-then-insert outside a transaction is insufficient.

Review and evidence

A deliberately incomplete design uses only a boolean running flag and has no crash recovery rule. The reference records enough state to recover authority after a crash. The database test demonstrates expiry, redelivery, stale rejection, one database effect, cancellation, and retry delay. It does not test arbitrary external effects, distributed clock skew, or sustained queue growth. Cancellation is best understood as a request that prevents future accepted completion under this database protocol, not as time travel.

Playbook investigation

Observation: jobs remain running longer than five seconds. Misleading evidence: the worker logged a successful claim. Hypotheses include no new claim scan, clock rollback, a long transaction, or an incorrect deadline comparison. Inspect persisted timestamps and run claim with a controlled later timestamp in the isolated test. If it recovers immediately, the durable transition logic works for that case and “corrupted job row” is disproven. Trace the worker's next polling point and clock source. Keep the fix narrow and document what happens during a future clock jump.

Mastery check

Implement heartbeat renewal without the reference, prove a stale token cannot renew, and explain why the same token rule must be checked at the resource that performs the effect. Provide one intentionally failing test that demonstrates the old design's defect.

When you get stuck

Run the scheduler PostgreSQL test explicitly. Query the isolated jobs row for status, attempts, token, due, and lease_until. Compare those observations with your transition table. In a review request include both worker timelines and the effect boundary; a timestamp alone does not explain authority.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Scope and invariants: one local worker; at-least-once leases; three attempts maximum;10,000 retained jobs; exact duplicate submission is harmless; current token and unexpired authority are required for completion. The only reference effect is a database row committed with completion. Why this design: PostgreSQL supplies durable uniqueness, locks, and atomic updates, while an explicit token makes stale-worker behavior testable. The admission advisory lock serializes only the small local queue's count-and-insert decision. Concrete habits: preserve logical IDs; reject conflicting payloads; use deterministic times in tests; propagate invalid system-clock errors instead of silently inventing a timestamp.

Alternative: a dedicated broker can supply delivery operations, but the application still owns effect idempotency and retention. A transactional counter can avoid repeatedly counting retained rows when measured enqueue throughput justifies more complexity. Evidence: actual database tests exercise expiry, fencing, cancellation, retries, deduplication, and full-budget admission. No external exactly-once guarantee or multi-host clock result is claimed. Evolution threshold: before multiple hosts, define a time authority, fair work selection, heartbeat limits, deployment connection/rate budgets, retention, and downstream effect contracts.

The API also admits at most16 handlers and imposes a five-second request/body deadline. Its runtime pool uses a three-second acquisition timeout and per-connection PostgreSQL statement timeout, so a worker blocked on database work has a finite statement wait before it can observe shutdown. The tests use isolated test pools; these operational settings are visible in the executable rather than asserted as database-server global configuration. A timeout remains an uncertain outcome; preserve the logical job ID when reconciling.

Reconstruct this runnable checkpoint

Working directory: course root. This creates a complete separate source tree; it refuses an existing destination. Run the checkpoint tests before following the guided edits. The checkpoint contract and engineering decisions state exactly which features exist.

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p14 final
mise exec -- cargo test --locked --manifest-path learner-work/checkpoints/p14-scheduler/final/Cargo.toml

To compare an earlier milestone with the final reference, reconstruct each ID into a different directory. The final database integration checks still require the explicitly isolated database described in this lesson; ordinary cargo test does not execute ignored database tests.

Investigate a lease that aged while waiting

Observation: a worker started completion before its lease expired but waited for a database row lock. A tempting hypothesis is that the fencing token alone makes the old timestamp safe. The delayed-lock test holds the row in another transaction, waits until PostgreSQL reports an actual blocked lock request, advances the injected clock to expiry, and releases the row. Completion returns false and produces no effect. It would wrongly accept if it sampled time before waiting. No guessed sleep is used to establish the interleaving.

The post-lock clock sample is the authority decision time, not a claim about every later hardware write. Once accepted, the same transaction retains the lock while writing the database effect. Clock rollback, multi-host time authority and external effects still need additional contracts. complete(pool, lease, now) and fail(pool, lease, now) remain logical-time APIs for deterministic models. The live worker does not call fail; its local database effect is attempted immediately and an uncertain storage failure leaves the job to expire. For completion, deployed workers should use the clock callback path rather than taking a stale timestamp before an asynchronous wait.

The conditional retry UPDATE computes its delay from the stored attempts column. A bounded integer shift gives 2,000, 4,000 and 8,000 milliseconds; the third failure becomes dead. The numeric intermediate and upper clamp prevent overflowing the signed timestamp on addition. Read the PostgreSQL 18 integer operator documentation and identify which cast preserves integer semantics. This arithmetic is part of an atomic predicate/update, not a Rust value supplied by the worker.

Test the API boundary before database work

The reusable router is in src/http.rs; main owns the pool, worker and shutdown. The loopback test supplies a lazy pool, sends real HTTP requests, and checks absent/unknown fixture identity, invalid inputs, malformed JSON, body limits and health. Denied mutations return before any database query. A public fixture token is still not production authentication, and a healthy route still does not prove database readiness.

mise exec -- cargo test -p p14-scheduler --test http
# With the explicitly isolated scheduler test URL:
mise exec -- cargo test -p p14-scheduler --test postgres -- --ignored

The database test executable serializes its fixtures with a mutex because they share disposable teaching tables. Do not start another copy against the same fixture database concurrently. The author verification used a fresh Unix-socket-only PostgreSQL cluster and removed it after shutdown; it did not alter an existing database.

Protect the disposable test boundary

The scheduler's opt-in database tests require the exact name rust_course_test_scheduler and a literal loopback address or absolute local socket path. A shared test helper parses the effective SQLx connection options and verifies SELECT current_database() on every new connection before migrations or resets. A string containing the test name elsewhere in a URL is insufficient. Tests still require a database you have established is disposable; the name and local transport alone do not establish ownership. The author verification creates a fresh private Unix-socket-only cluster and removes only that cluster after a successful shutdown.

Output policy and ownership at process boundaries

The listener bind and required startup banner now complete before spawning the worker. A closed stdout pipe is ordinary I/O failure; startup uses writeln! and flush with ? instead of a panic-producing printing macro. SCHEDULER_DATABASE_URL errors use a fixed message because the non-Unicode error type can otherwise retain the original credential-bearing value.

Worker observations have a different contract: they use best-effort Write calls, and an output error does not panic the task or decide whether a database effect committed. That means a lost log line is possible. Inspect durable job/effect state when reconciling outcomes; a log line is not a durable acknowledgment or audit record. A synchronous write can still block on a slow sink. This small local demonstration does not promise a hard shutdown deadline for logging; a stronger operational requirement would justify a bounded logging worker and an explicit dropped-message policy.

The main task owns the Ctrl-C future and a pinned server future. The same watch sender can stop both the server and worker. Every server exit signals the worker, awaits its handle, closes the pool, and only then returns saved server, worker or signal errors. It no longer uses an early ? after serving that could skip the join. The worker observes the current stop state before waiting, so an already-set stop is effective. Read the process evidence and remaining limits; a source review of this ordering is distinct from an injected accept-error execution.

title: A deterministic replicated-state laboratory
summary: Test narrow safety and liveness properties without claiming production consensus.
objectives: Define safety versus liveness precisely
Explore partitions, loss, delay and restart deterministically
Identify assumptions missing from a consensus protocol
body:
Purpose and specification first

Build a deterministic simulator with three nodes and a permanent leader, node0. Only the leader may propose values. It assigns each value its next log index. Followers append only the next missing index and acknowledge an identical duplicate. A conflicting value at an existing index cannot overwrite it. The leader calls a prefix committed after acknowledgments from any two nodes. There is no leader election, membership change, real networking, real disk, malicious-node model, or claim to implement Raft.

Plain-English model: events instead of wall time

A simulator turns uncertain timing into explicit choices. A queue holds message objects. A step delivers or drops one object according to current node and partition state. Delay moves a packet to the end; loss removes it; crash makes a node unavailable while preserving its simulated durable vector. “Durable” here means the model preserves it across the simulator's restart action. It does not mean bytes reached a disk or survived a power failure.

A safety property says something bad never happens. Here, every follower's log must remain a prefix of the fixed leader's log, and existing entries must never change. A liveness property says something good eventually happens under explicit assumptions. Here, after the leader and one follower are online, their link is healed, and resend/delivery continues, proposed entries can reach a two-node acknowledgment count. A permanent partition can prevent progress. No amount of local type checking promises communication eventually succeeds.

Prediction

Partition the leader from both followers, propose42, and drain the queue. Has42 been committed? Heal only the link to follower1, resend, and drain again. Does follower2 need to be online for progress?

Answer

The first committed count is0. The leader's local append alone is not a two-node acknowledgment. After one follower receives and acknowledges the entry, the count becomes1. The second follower may remain isolated. This illustrates a quorum in this model, not a complete theorem about arbitrary leader changes.

Small runnable example

Working directory: rust-course/projects. This project uses only the standard library and the pinned compiler.

mise exec -- cargo run -p p15-replication
mise exec -- cargo test -p p15-replication

Expected output reports committed0 while partitioned and committed1 after healing, with prefix safety true in both cases. A system can remain safe while unavailable. Availability is not proved by a safety assertion.

Guided construction

Start with Node, Message, Packet, and an empty Lab. Implement leader proposal and an append-only follower rule. Test duplicate append before adding acknowledgments. Then add an acknowledgment set per index and advance the committed prefix only while every earlier index has enough acknowledgments. This last condition matters: receiving acknowledgment for a later position should not skip an uncommitted hole.

The reference resend action clears queued packets and emits the leader's current history to followers. This is a deterministic recovery shortcut, not a realistic network retransmission layer. It makes repeated healing experiments simple, but you must keep that simplification in any claimed liveness result. A production log would also need bounded replication windows, snapshots, persistent term/index metadata, and a specified recovery algorithm.

Deliberate mistake

Change the follower to append every received value regardless of index. Deliver the same append twice. The follower now has extra history and the prefix property fails. Restore the index rule. Then deliberately accept a conflicting duplicate by overwriting an existing entry. The conflict test exposes another safety violation. Neither bug requires unsafe Rust.

Independent experiments

Enumerate schedules containing two proposals, one dropped packet, one crash, and one restart. State a finite bound on steps and assert safety after every action, not only after drain. Add a new invariant that committed never decreases. Decide what should happen if the leader restarts and forgets acknowledgment sets while retaining its log. Do not add a new leader until you have written a protocol for authority and conflicting history.

Hint 1

Represent actions as data so a failing schedule can be printed and replayed exactly.

Hint 2

A safety check should run after each transition. A final converged state can hide an earlier temporary violation.

Reference reasoning

Use a bounded depth-first enumeration over a small action alphabet, prune impossible node indices, and retain the shortest failing sequence. For leader restart, reconstruct or reacquire acknowledgments and avoid reporting old commitment from unverified volatile state. The reference keeps acknowledgment state in the simulator, so changing that assumption is a genuine model extension.

Review and evidence

A misleading demonstration sends messages in perfect order and calls the result consensus. This lab explicitly perturbs delivery and states what it does not implement. Its tests check a finite family of schedules, duplicate behavior, conflict rejection, and recovery after healing. They do not constitute exhaustive model checking, a proof of linearizability, or validation of real network and disk code. Study the original Raft paper before designing election, terms, voting, or log reconciliation; do not infer those rules from this simplified fixed-leader model.

Playbook investigation

Observation: the leader reports no progress after healing. A tempting guess is that majority replication requires all three nodes. Inspect the queue and acknowledgments. If the lost append was never resent, the missing assumption is continued retransmission, not a three-node quorum. Schedule one explicit resend and see whether two acknowledgments suffice. That experiment disproves the all-nodes hypothesis for this model. If progress still fails, inspect out-of-order indices and dropped acknowledgments separately rather than changing quorum size until the test passes.

Mastery check

Explain the exact safety invariant, liveness assumptions, and simulated durability boundary. Produce a failing schedule for a deliberate bug, then fix it and retain the regression. Identify three additional mechanisms needed before this could reasonably be called a consensus implementation.

When you get stuck

Run mise exec -- cargo test -p p15-replication duplicates_restarts_delay_and_loss -- --nocapture. Print each action with queue and logs only in your learner copy. Compare the first divergence against the prefix invariant. Ask for review with a minimal replayable schedule and the precise property; “it sometimes disagrees” is not enough.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Scope and invariants: three simulated nodes, one permanent leader,1,000 log entries, bounded resend queue, immutable indexed entries, and follower-prefix safety. Simulated restart retains model state; no disk semantics are implied. Why this design: representing delivery decisions as data creates reproducible failures without wall-clock races. Concrete habits: name a precise property; assert it after transitions; preserve failing schedules; state fairness and delivery assumptions separately from safety.

Alternative: use a model checker and a formal specification for broader state exploration; use an established consensus implementation for an actual replicated service. The educational simulator exposes its state for experiments and does not validate arbitrary malicious packets or node indices as an Internet service would. Evidence: finite schedule tests establish the tested schedules only. Evolution threshold: leader change, membership change, persisted term metadata, or Byzantine participants require a new protocol specification and evidence, not a renamed function or an additional happy-path test.

A small demonstration still handles its boundaries

The simulator entry point prints through a locked stdout Write implementation and returns an I/O result, so a closed pipe is an ordinary error instead of a panic.
